items.title: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
items.summary: Leaked data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia.
items.content:
Image caption, Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiers
By Olga Ivshina Â  and Â  Yaroslava Kiryukhina ,Â  BBC Russian
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years.
Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.
Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.
The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.
The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.
During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.
Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.
For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.
Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.
Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.
The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.
We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.
Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.
As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian â unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.
Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.
Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.
According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).
Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.
In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.
At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.
This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.
The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.
The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant.
In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.
In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.

Iran Reports Fresh Tanker Explosions as Hormuz Attacks Intensify
Two oil tankers exploded early on Wednesday after hitting naval mines while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz on routes unauthorized by Iran, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said.
These Iranian reports about tankers that Tehran says are 'violating' the Iranian terms of navigation through the chokepoint have become a nearly daily occurrence in the past few weeks.
Two tankers hit naval mines off the southern and eastern coasts of the Strait of Hormuz early on Wednesday, resulting in fires erupting in their engine rooms, the IRGC said in a statement carried by Iranian news agency IRNA.
"These oil tankers imagined they were secretly passing through the fake route of the Strait of Hormuz, but the naval mines blocked their passage, setting off a massive explosion and fire," the IRGC Navy said.
"The IRGC Navy's Strait of Hormuz Traffic Control Center warned all crews of ships with their navigation and positioning systems switched off to be careful that American officials' lies do not drag them into the explosion and fire of naval mines."
Earlier this week, Iran said three other tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines after violating regulations and instructions from the IRGC Navy Traffic Control Center.
Iran has intensified attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks, just as crude oil flows from the Persian Gulf recover and oil prices fall amid expectations of oversupply within months.
The number of attacks soared in October to the highest level since the Iran war began at the end of February, and has continued at nearly daily occurrences so far in November, according to data compiled by Bloomberg .
Meanwhile, crude oil volumes flowing from the Strait of Hormuz have declined in recent days, although it's unclear if this is entirely due to the more frequent attacks on tankers.

Iran Protests & Demonstrations Iran Economy News Iranian Regime Infighting
Iran’s Regime Warns of Internal Collapse as Truckers’ Strike Spreads and Rial Hits New Low
Homa (Iran Air) retirees gather in Tehran on October 27, 2026, to protest pension and livelihood conditions amid Iran’s deepening economic crisis
Speaking at a gathering attended by senior security figures, including Basij commander Hossein Taeb, the Iranian regime's president Masoud Pezeshkian warned that no foreign power could overthrow the establishment unless its own conduct undermined it.
He urged regime officials to stop attacking and labeling one another and to show greater willingness to compromise. His appeal came amid chants pledging loyalty to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and denouncing the regime's opponents.
The warning was directed at rival factions rather than an acknowledgment of the regime's responsibility for the crisis. Pezeshkian appears increasingly concerned that infighting and economic hardship could create conditions for another nationwide uprising, but remains careful to frame his appeals within declarations of loyalty to the leadership.
Truck drivers continued their strike Wednesday for a fourth consecutive day, according to reports circulated by labor and opposition networks.
With drivers in Kazerun reportedly joining the action, the strike has now been reported in 16 cities, including Tehran, Shiraz, Isfahan, Bandar Abbas, Ahvaz, Kermanshah, Qazvin, Chabahar and Sirjan.
Iran, Nov. 24: The rial hits another record low as retirees in Kermanshah chant, “We want neither war nor killing; we want lasting welfare.” State newspapers expose soaring costs, pension-fund deficits and medicine shortages. A political analyst warns another nationwide…
The drivers are protesting inadequate freight rates, fuel shortages and sharply rising costs for tires, spare parts and vehicle maintenance. Their continued defiance follows official denials that any strike is taking place, highlighting the widening discrepancy between government assurances and the grievances driving labor unrest.
Meanwhile, retirees from Iran Air demonstrated outside the Ministry of Roads in Tehran. Welfare Organization employees protested in Karaj, while electricity-sector workers reportedly gathered outside the Energy Ministry in Tehran over employment-related grievances.
Iran's currency suffered another steep decline Wednesday, with the dollar reaching approximately 290,500 tomans in the unofficial market during afternoon trading.
According to market figures, the dollar has risen by nearly 18,000 tomans in just two days.
Pezeshkian keeps publicly warning of winter energy crises, oil-sale blockages & #IranProtests . Hardliners (and Mojtaba Khamenei) want him to stop “advertising weakness.” He might be more worried about an unprepared population exploding than about signaling vulnerability abroad.…
The latest depreciation coincided with new US sanctions targeting 29 individuals and entities, including institutions involved in Iran's foreign-exchange operations.
As authorities attempted to reassure markets, the state-affiliated Fars news agency claimed that a substantial shipment of dollar banknotes had entered Iran from a neighboring country.
The falling rial further threatens household purchasing power and raises the cost of imported goods and essential production inputs.
Economic Contraction Deepens Across Oil and Industry
Wednesday's Donya-e Eqtesad reported that industrial and mining output contracted by an estimated 10% during the summer.
Production among listed industrial companies fell 12.5% year-on-year in September, while inventories of finished industrial goods declined by 8%.
Iran, Nov. 21: Bread controls now operate in seven provinces as bakers protest and fuel queues persist. Workers, students and consumers demonstrate, while #Abdanan arrests rise to 12. Tehran faces renewed blackout fears, and Pezeshkian acknowledges failing enterprises and…
The figures suggest that factories are struggling not merely with weak demand but with shortages of raw materials, energy disruptions, foreign-exchange restrictions and difficulties importing essential components.
Separately, Setareh Sobh reported that Iran's economy contracted by an estimated 5.2%, with the oil sector registering particularly severe losses.
Oil-sector activity fell 31.7% year-on-year in September, according to estimates cited by the newspaper, underscoring the economic consequences of the blockade and prolonged confrontation.
Pezeshkian has announced plans to reorganize flour and bread subsidies, contradicting recent assurances that subsidized bread prices and allocations would remain unchanged.
Authorities have already imposed purchasing restrictions on approximately 280,000 national identification numbers across seven provinces under a program targeting what officials call abnormal bread consumption.
Iran, Nov. 23: Truckers' strike enters day two despite official denials. Telecom retirees, workers and investors protest as producer #inflation reaches 120.9% and industrial prices jump 147.3%. State newspapers warn of deepening economic misery while regime factions clash over…
In a pointed warning, Ebtekar criticized the proposed bread-rationing measures under the headline Do Not Deprive Workers of Even Plain Bread , warning that restricting access to subsidized bread would further undermine the livelihoods of impoverished workers and pave the way for unrest.
The controversy exposes the regime's approach to its fiscal crisis: instead of resolving the policies driving inflation and poverty, it is increasingly restricting access to the cheapest necessities on which impoverished families depend.
Hardliners Demand Confrontation as Mediation Continues
While Qatar continues efforts to revive negotiations between Tehran and Washington, the regime's hardline camp is escalating its opposition to compromise. In a Wednesday editorial , Kayhan directly attacked calls for diplomatic efforts to end the American naval blockade, declaring that the blockade must be broken through force rather than concessions.
The intervention followed the failure of widely publicized claims that Iranian oil tankers would challenge the blockade.
Meanwhile, Shargh published an extensive interview with Hossein Marashi, secretary-general of the Executives of Construction Party, who warned that the country could not credibly claim to prioritize livelihoods while imposing inflation of approximately 90% on its population.
"The factions are not simply arguing over appointments or electoral advantage. They are fighting over #diplomacy , economic policy, the presidency, parliament and the security apparatus—while each insists that its own course is necessary to preserve the ruling establishment,"…
Marashi portrayed Iran's costly regional confrontation as a strategic achievement, calling for its military gains to be consolidated through "diplomacy."
His remarks exposed a contradiction within the establishment: even as so-called "reformist" figures acknowledge the devastating economic consequences of the regime's policies, they continue to defend its regional ambitions and seek ways to preserve the existing power structure rather than question its foundations.
New Internet-Control Plan Raises Surveillance Concerns
A Wednesday Ham-Mihan report warned that a new draft framework for governing cyberspace revives central elements of the controversial internet-restriction legislation.
The proposed measures would expand government oversight of foreign platforms, international internet traffic and communications infrastructure.
The initiative comes despite repeated public demands for fewer internet restrictions and amid growing concern about the regime's ability to monitor dissent.
Iran, Nov. 20: Labor representatives say wages cover barely 10 days of living costs. Reports emerge of two protesters' death sentences being upheld. #Bread queues grow, transport costs rise and officials warn of winter blackouts. Meanwhile, the regime expands Basij mobilization…
The developments reveal a ruling establishment increasingly alarmed by the consequences of its own policies. Pezeshkian warns that internal divisions could threaten its survival, while hardliners demand further confrontation and security institutions seek greater control over communications.
Outside the corridors of power, truckers continue their strike, workers demand unpaid benefits and families struggle with a collapsing currency and increasingly unaffordable necessities.
The regime's central predicament is not simply an economic downturn or factional rivalry. Its confrontational policies are deepening the crisis, while the political concessions needed to ease public anger threaten the foundations of the system it is determined to preserve.

Oil Prices Slide Despite Mounting Threats in the Strait of Hormuz
Oil prices extended their losses following a modest reported build in U.S. crude inventories.
Oversupply fears and hopes for peace negotiations are overshadowing threats to tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
Persistent disagreements between Washington and Tehran leave oil markets vulnerable to renewed geopolitical volatility.
Crude oil prices moved lower in early Asian trading on Wednesday, extending the recent downward trend despite reports of increasingly frequent incidents involving tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, with Iranian authorities attributing them to mines and other sources suggesting strikes with projectiles.
At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $90.10 per barrel, with West Texas Intermediate at $80.71, after the American Petroleum Institute reported a modest build in U.S. crude oil inventories, at 126,000 barrels for the week to November 20.
The oil market appears to be once again dominated by the optimists taking the view that escalation in the Middle East is unlikely, even though oil export rates are down from September, according to Kpler data.
“Since the release of an IEA report this month, perceptions of a global supply glut have kept prices in check,” Tsuyoshi Ueno, senior economist at NLI Research Institute, said as quoted by Reuters this week.
“However, attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz and exchanges of attacks between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis have raised uncertainty over the sustainability of this trend,” the analyst added.
ING commodity analysts, meanwhile, noted that expectations of peace negotiations were also keeping prices depressed. “The prospect of negotiations has eased some immediate concerns over Middle East supply, particularly as crude exports from the Persian Gulf have remained relatively resilient despite continued disruption around the Strait of Hormuz,
Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote. “However, significant differences between the US and Iran remain, leaving oil vulnerable to any setback in talks.”
Iran and the United States have had irreconcilable differences from the start, and neither has budged on their demands from the other, making the peace negotiation process highly fraught. This has so far not deterred oil traders from taking the optimistic view, but the possibility of escalation, as suggested by President Trump, may change that.

items.summary: Market sell-off eases up, but AI doubts, tariffs and inflation still weigh down stocks  NBC News<a href="https://news.google.com/rss/articles/C
items.content:
Wednesday's losses marked a stark reversal from Monday, when financial markets staged their biggest one-day rally since April 2025. John Lamparski / Bloomberg via Getty
Nov. 25, 2026, 10:24 AM EST  /  Updated   Nov. 25, 2026, 1:36 PM EST
U.S. stocks broadly slumped Wednesday, led by companies linked to the AI boom.
The volatile day began with a sharp sell-off that briefly sent the influential Nasdaq 100 index into bear market territory, which occurs when an index falls by 20% or more from its most recent high. The S&P 500 was down by as much as 3.2% in early trading.
But sentiment among traders and investors improved slightly over the course of the day.
An early beneficiary of the renewed optimism was Anthropic, the AI giant that staged a record-setting IPO last week, only to see its stock battered for three straight trading sessions. Shortly after midday, Anthropic was finally trading back above its IPO price of $83 per share.
Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite was down roughly 1.5% and the S&P 500 was lower by only 0.5%. The Dow was flat in early afternoon trading and just barely back over a symbolic 50,000.
Even as markets pulled back from their lows, Nvidia remained among the biggest losers in key indexes. After soaring by 31% on Monday on news that its recently-departed CEO Jensen Huang would return to the C-suite, the stock was still lower by about 7% Wednesday, its second straight down day.

The return of Huang, a de facto ambassador for the artificial intelligence industry, briefly reassured investors that big AI firms, and the trillions of dollars they borrow and lend, would continue to grow without interruption.
Stock markets Monday staged their biggest one-day rally since April 2025, as the Nasdaq 100 skyrocketed 6.8% and the S&P 500 surged 4.7%.
President Donald Trump pushed Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang over the weekend despite multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Before the president stepped in, the board had been unequivocal that it did not plan to reinstate Huang.
Trump said Monday that he “probably” decided to intervene in Nvidia’s internal leadership decision because he was concerned about a market sell-off in the week after Huang’s departure fueled partly by investor concerns about how the CEO’s resignation would impact the broader AI industry.
But ever since Monday’s rally, markets have struggled to maintain that upward momentum.
“The risk-off tone has returned over the last 24 hours, as Monday’s rebound in tech stocks lost momentum once again,” Deutsche Bank strategists said in a note early Wednesday.
Before Monday’s one-day rally, stocks had faced weeks of selling, which pushed the Nasdaq 100 into correction territory on Friday, which is defined as a 10% drop from its last high.

Shares of semiconductor stocks, as tracked by the Philadelphia semiconductor index, have plunged more than 40% since their last peak in June. Stocks of companies that make data center and computer memory products have plummeted 60% over the same period.
AI-related sentiment has also been damaged further by frontier developer Anthropic, whose shares have spiraled lower since its initial public offering last week.
Stocks Wednesday likely faced additional pressure due to the looming Thanksgiving holiday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday and open for only a half-day of trading Friday.
Investors are more likely to cut their large or risky trades before extended weekends, in order to avoid being trapped in positions while events unfold.
On top of cracks in the AI sector, “matters weren’t helped by the latest tariff headlines,” Deutsche Bank’s team wrote.
On Wednesday, t he Trump administration unveiled a new wave of tariffs on the United States’ top trading partners, such as the European Union, China, Japan and a dozen more.
“It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind,” ING senior trade economist Inga Fechner wrote in a note Wednesday.
That drove stocks down further, with the prospect that more tariffs could cause renewed trade tensions, a renewed inflation spike and cause a flare-up with a policy that had largely started to subside in recent months.
Even before Wednesday’s formal announcement, a spokesperson for the Chinese Commerce Ministry blasted the new import duties. “Tariff wars and trade wars are in the interests of neither side,” the spokesperson said. The ministry called it “political manipulation.”
“Some investors might have been caught off guard by news that the Administration is on track to release more tariffs, but the key question about the Administration unveiling new tariffs from the Section 301 overcapacity investigation has never been an issue of whether but when,” wrote Sarah Bianchi, chief strategist of international political affairs at Evercore ISI.
Compounding the negative pressure facing investors Wednesday, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge moved further away from its 2% goal.
The personal consumption expenditures index was 3.8% for October, up from 3.6% in September. Even excluding food and energy, the “core” inflation reading rose to 3.3%. It had been 3.1% the previous month.
The rise in core inflation readings is particularly noteworthy because it can indicate that higher gas prices sparked by the Iran war are spilling over into the rest of the economy.
It also raises the likelihood that the Fed will raise interest rates at its next meeting, which concludes with a rate decision Dec. 9.
Last week, a top Fed policymaker said the central bank needed to “shock people” with a larger rate hike than is typical.
“I’m very, very concerned about inflation,” Fed governor Christopher Waller said in a CNBC interview . “It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.”
Waller said the Fed needed to take “more aggressive actions,” such as hiking by 0.50%, more than the Fed’s usual 0.25% rate increase. “You might need to, like, shock people,” he said.
A rate hike would carry its own complications, however. As trillion-dollar tech giants borrow hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI data centers and chips, any increase to interest rates could quickly raise their massive costs.
It could also hurt an already pained U.S. consumer. Mortgage rates continue to hover well above 7%, and a rate hike could push borrowing costs higher for auto loans, credit cards, personal loans and other forms of credit.

items.title: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
items.summary: Swiss officials said relations would be kept through North Korea's embassy in Bern, and its own embassy in Beijing.
items.content:
Image caption, Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang
North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close amid a row over sanctions.
It said the move was in response to Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp. State media described this as "a blatant hostile act".
That camp is at the centre of claims that it was involved in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.
North Korea's foreign ministry said "any act of violating the sovereign rights" of the country and the interests of its citizens "can never be welcomed".
Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.
Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.
The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.
Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997.
Image caption, A Swiss delegation, on left, including Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis, met with North Korean officials in Pyongyang last month
Switzerland's federal department of foreign affairs said the country "distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries".
It added: "The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine."
Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been deployed to help support Russia's war with Ukraine.
In August, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

items.title: Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks
items.summary: The US president's intercession to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang has inextricably linked their fates.
items.content:
Figure caption, Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?
After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.
"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.
Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised fist clenching a red bra.
The post was classic Trump â potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.
Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal â one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy â the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?
Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?
At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.
And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.
While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter.
"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".
Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.
They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.
State governments could also launch their own investigations.
Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing â and, by association, Trump himself.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.
Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump
US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.
Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.
Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large.
In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.
"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.
The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.
Figure caption, How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO
The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.
Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.
Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year.
The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.
Trump's decision to help save Huang â noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" â could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.
"It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday.
"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."
For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.
Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy.
He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic).
And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.
Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters.
He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI â which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" â will control the fate of the world.
If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.
In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%.
US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.
The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble â like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 â that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.
Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.
On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.
Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed.
And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

items.title: More than 490,000 Russian soldiers have died during Ukraine war, leaked data suggests - CBS News
items.summary: More than 490,000 Russian soldiers have died during Ukraine war, leaked data suggests  CBS News
items.content:
More than 490,000 Russian soldiers have died since Vladimir Putin ordered Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, according to leaked Russian government data analyzed by CBS News partner network BBC News . Another organization's analysis of the vast dataset suggests the toll is likely closer to 700,000.
A recent hack by pro-Ukraine groups Belarusian Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow produced the data that was analyzed by the BBC and independent Russian outlet Mediazona. It included more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, according to the British broadcaster.
The data, which includes granular information on the location of deaths in Ukraine and Russian border regions, age ranges, causes of death, and employment and court rulings suggests at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died during the war so far, according to the BBC. According to Mediazona's analysis, which the outlet said accounted for delays in death registrations, missing records and deaths occurring since the data was leaked, Russia's total military death toll has likely reached around 700,000.
In May, the head of the United Kingdom's communications and cyber spy agency also put the number of Russian military deaths during the war at about 500,000, citing Western intelligence.
"Putin is going backwards on the battlefield, with new intelligence showing that almost half a million Russian soldiers have been killed since the conflict began," Anne Keast-Butler, the director of the Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ), said at the time.
Soldiers carry the coffin of 20-year-old Russian serviceman Nikita Avrov during his funeral at a church in Luga, south of St. Petersburg, April 11, 2022, after his death during the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine.
The Kremlin has not publicly revealed the Russian death toll from the war. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said for the first time in February that his country's losses stood at 55,000. The BBC also reported that the leaked data shows 65% of 18- to 24-year-olds in Russia who died in 2025 were casualties of the war. For Russians aged 25-34 last year, the number was 59%, making the war the main cause of death for young Russian adults last year, according to the data.
When asked about the various reports surfacing from the data leak, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday: "The only entity that can officially disclose casualty figures is the Defense Ministry of the Russian Federation."
"I suggest not to pay attention to any other data," he said.

items.title: My family were killed in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated
items.summary: BBC journalist Anastasiya Gribanova investigates who killed her father and grandparents in the war.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: BBC reporter investigates deaths of family members in Russia-Ukraine war
I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.
The woman who sent me the photo says the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.
Image caption, The photo Anastasiya was sent of her grandparents' graves
I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.
"Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it said.
Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.
Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.
Image caption, Anastasiya (bottom left) with her father (top left) and grandparents (right) before the war
Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.
After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.
Now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground , external .
Image source, Ukraine's 33rd Mechanised Brigade
Image caption, The remains of Anastasiya's family home are circled in a frame of a video, filmed by Ukraine's 33rd Mechanised Brigade on 27 January 2025
I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off.
But earlier this year, around the first anniversary of dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing dad just as much as I was.
Image caption, Anastasiya's father Serezha - he stayed in Dachne to look after his elderly parents
I told her I wanted to make a documentary about dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet.
I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals.
Russia publicly announced the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since.
This meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours.
Image caption, Anastasiya could not safely travel back to Dachne, so she worked through contacts in village group chats
In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call.
Misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he said.
It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time.
"I asked if the wound was serious. He [Serezha] said it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead.
With the help of two other villagers, Misha said they had buried him in the greenhouse.
"I'm sorry I couldn't save him," Misha told me.
BBC journalist Anastasiya Gribanova investigates who killed her father and grandparents in Ukraine, uncovering painful accounts as she tries to reunite her divided family.
Watch on BBC iPlayer or listen on BBC Sounds now (UK only)
If you are outside of the UK, listen to the Who Killed My Family podcast here
As for my grandparents, my investigations suggested the events surrounding their deaths may have been more complicated.
Their house, on the eastern side of Dachne, had been destroyed. Neighbours told me they had escaped to another home on the same street.
I eventually reached a woman I'll call Lina, who lived nearby and was the last person, as far as I know, who saw my grandparents alive.
She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January.
At this time, she said, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones."
She said two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians.
"You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina said they had asked her.
She said one had pointed a machine gun at her as she had stood outside her house, while another had gone to see my grandparents. She told me she had feared for her life and then fled her house for the night.
The following day, she told me she had returned to my grandparents' street to check on them.
She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she said, despite the freezing conditions.
With drones buzzing overhead, Lina said she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them.
Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood.
Maria also believed Ukrainian soldiers had killed them - because, she said, that she too had felt threatened by Ukrainian troops at the time.
"If they had seen me they would have killed me too."
Her theory was that my grandparents had irritated the troops in some way.
"Your grandparents caught them in a bad mood because your grandfather was always asking to be evacuated. And [the soldiers] were, you know, high. They were taking drugs. So your grandparents got in their way," she told me.
Most of the other people in the village I spoke to also believe Ukrainian soldiers killed them, though their testimony is not based on direct evidence.
The new local mayor, appointed by the Russian occupiers when they finally took control of Dachne in February, said she had been present at my grandparents' burial the following month, and said half of my grandmother's skull was missing.
These accounts of how they might have died in January 2025 were deeply disturbing, though no-one had witnessed their deaths and the information I was given could not be independently verified.
The villagers I spoke to - now living in occupied territory - did say there had been some tensions between themselves and Ukrainian troops at the time, because the soldiers had viewed those who remained in Dachne as supporters of Russia.
The clinical causes of my grandparents' deaths are unclear.
Their bodies were not exhumed for nearly 20 months, when the local authorities sent them to a morgue in the occupied region, where a basic autopsy was carried out by a forensics expert.
He told me that my grandmother had died of an explosives injury to the skull - but could not specify its cause.
As for my grandfather, it said his body had shown no obvious signs of injury.
I compared two satellite images of the house in which their bodies were found - from just before and just after when they are believed to have died - and could detect no significant damage to the building in the second image.
I also spoke to a villager who said he had buried my grandparents.
He said he did not know anything about who killed them.
"I wasn't there. But why would you kill old people?" he asked.
Image caption, Anastasiya does not know if she will ever be able to give her grandparents (pictured) a dignified burial
I examined military maps from DeepStateMap.Live, an open-source Ukrainian resource, and US think tank Institute for the Study of War. They suggested Ukrainian forces still held the street where my grandparents lived during the week they had died, although the front line had been shifting rapidly.
My colleagues helped me identify the Russian military units that went on to capture Dachne. We found telephone numbers of Russian soldiers. But none of them agreed to speak to me.
A soldier from the 33rd Mechanised Brigade, who gave his name simply as Vlad, said his unit had still been in Dachne at the time my grandparents were believed to have died and that the Russians had been swiftly advancing.
Another Ukrainian soldier I spoke to also confirmed Ukraine's troops had still been in control of some parts of Dachne in late January.
We put our findings on the deaths of my grandparents to the Ukrainian military.
It said it had no verified evidence on how they died, or which implicated its servicemen during the "intense hostilities". It added that investigating allegations of wrongdoing was the role of law enforcement.
We also approached Russia's ministry of defence and Russia's embassy in London for comment - they did not respond.
Image caption, Sisters Sasha (right) and Anastasiya were reunited at Belgrade Airport
The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office, which is now based outside Russian-controlled territory, has documented alleged Russian war crimes reported by eyewitnesses in villages around Dachne during December 2024 and January 2025 - including the killing of five civilians in a basement in the nearby village of Kostyantynopilske.
However, Ukrainian investigators have no equivalent cases registered in Dachne during that period. They have documented only three deaths there. My father and grandparents are not among them.
Their bodies lie in occupied territory, and I do not know if I will ever be able to say goodbye properly and bury them with dignity.
There is little more I can do for them, except one thing - mend my relationship with my sister and my mother.
Almost three years after I last saw my sister, I fly to Belgrade where she now lives.
Image caption, Anastasiya (left) and her sister Sasha look through photos of their father
She is waiting for me at the airport, holding lilies, and a plate with a silly nickname on it that she gave me when we were children. We hug, cry and laugh. It feels as if something between us is finally falling back into place
At her flat, we look through family photographs and talk about my investigation and what I was able to find. My grief is still there, but it hurts a little less. I'm no longer carrying it alone.
"Are you ready?" Sasha asks. She rings our mother - who has also moved to Serbia - and puts the phone on speaker.
"Hi, Mum. It's Nastya," I say. First there is silence. Then I hear her crying. "Nastya, my darling, hello," she replies.

Ukraine tells Putin to 'stop complaining' over refinery attacks
Ukraine’s foreign minister told Putin to end the war if he wants Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries, after Russia's president said retaliation was “inevitable.”
Zelenskyy said Nov. 15 that Ukrainian strikes have disabled more than 55% of Russia’s oil-refining capacity.
Putin described Russia’s fuel supply situation as “challenging,” as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russian targets.
In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin holds a Security Council meeting in Moscow on November 6, 2026.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has told Russian President Vladimir Putin to "stop complaining" over attacks on Russian refineries, saying Putin could end Kyiv's strikes on the oil facilities by bringing an end to the Kremlin's nearly five-year-long war.
His comments come shortly after Russia's president told a meeting of government officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin on Tuesday that Ukraine continues to attack refining facilities despite U.S. President Donald Trump 's appeal to refrain from doing so.
"I would like to note that retaliatory action from our side is inevitable. Everyone must be aware of that," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency Tass .
In September, Trump called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks were " hurting the world " as fuel supply disruptions from the wars in Ukraine and Iran propelled U.S. diesel prices to a record high. Moscow welcomed Trump's push for Ukraine to halt strikes on Russia's diesel-producing facilities at the time.
"If Putin doesn't like Ukraine's strikes on his oil refineries, he can order an end to the war," Ukraine's Sybiha said Tuesday via social media.
"If he doesn't want his military vessels hit, he can order an end to the war. Not to mention the 432,000 Russian soldiers he has lost on the battlefield this year without coming any closer to the goals of his invasion. Clearly, he doesn't care about them. Stop complaining. End the war," he added. CNBC could not independently verify the figures.
In July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that about 1.4 million Russian troops were killed, wounded or went missing between the start of the full-scale invasion in Feb. 2022 and June 2026, with more than 30,000 casualties a month in the first half of this year.
Satellite view of thick black smoke rising from multiple fires at Rosneft's Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery in Samara Oblast, Russia, on October 30, 2026.
Ukraine has stepped up attacks on Russian critical targets in recent weeks, damaging Putin's prized Crimea bridge , striking a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea and destroying one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port .
Kyiv has also targeted Russian energy infrastructure . Zelenskyy said earlier this month that Ukraine's long-range strikes had disabled more than 55% of Russia's oil-refining capacity, describing this as a "justified response to Russia's refusal to de-escalate and its strikes on our energy infrastructure."
Putin: Fuel supply situation remains 'challenging'
Ukrainian drones reportedly struck two major Russian oil refineries in Russia's Samara region overnight, triggering fires at both facilities.
Satellite images published in late October also showed black smoke rising from multiple fires at Rosneft's Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in southern Russia following a suspected Ukrainian drone attack.
Putin on Tuesday said Russia's fuel market situation remains "challenging" and called on government officials and oil executives "to continue reacting promptly to the supply-demand relationship for fuel across the whole territory of Russia," according to Interfax .
Ukraine's allies have warned the country faces another winter of blackouts and freezing temperatures amid escalating Russian energy strikes.

PCE inflation report October 2026: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8%
The personal consumption expenditures price index rose by a seasonally adjusted 3.8% annual rate in October, nearly twice the Federal Reserve’s target.
Excluding food and energy, so-called core PCE was 3.3%, the Commerce Department said.
The headline number was in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate, while core PCE was 0.1 percentage point above the forecast.
Fed’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8% in October, likely sealing rate hike
Inflation moved further away from the Federal Reserve's target in October, reinforcing expectations that another interest rate hike is in the cards for December and raising questions about how much more work the central bank will have to do in 2027.
The personal consumption expenditures price index , the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed a seasonally adjusted 3.8% annual inflation rate, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate and nearly twice the central bank's goal. The reading was 0.1 percentage point higher than September.
Excluding food and energy, core PCE was 3.3%, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday. That was 0.1 percentage point above the forecast.
While the Fed officially follows the headline figure, policymakers consider core to be a more reliable longer-term gauge of inflation trends.
A separate report also showed much stronger economic growth for the third quarter, with gross domestic product rising at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate. The strong top-line gain for the economy adds further fuel to the notion that Fed monetary policy is not restricting economic activity.
Consumer spending rose 0.3% for the month, which matched the pace of price increases but was 0.1 percentage point lower than forecast. Income, on the other hand, surged 0.7%, much more than the 0.4% estimate. The personal saving rate rose to 4.1%.
Stock market futures added to losses following the release, while Treasury yields also were sharply lower. Even with the higher-than-expected core inflation figure, expectations eased a bit for Fed rate hikes in 2027. Traders continued to price in two more increases but lowered odds for a third hike to about 1-in-3, compared to 50-50 on Tuesday, according to the CME Group's FedWatch .
"Inflation is too hot and it will not be brought under control as long as economic demand is also too hot," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds.
The report comes with the market fully pricing in a quarter percentage point interest rate hike when the Fed meets Dec. 8-9. Less certain is how much more rates will need to increase to get inflation back down to the Fed's 2% target. Inflation has been running above target for some 5½ years.
Inflation had been drifting lower but spiked again following the late-February attacks on Iran led by the U.S. and Israel. Tariffs also have continued to exert pressure, as has strong demand associated with the artificial intelligence buildout. The White House on Wednesday announced a fresh round of tariffs on 14 trading partners including China, the European Union and Japan.
Policymakers generally consider factors such as tariffs and supply shocks to be temporary, but some fear the impact has begun spreading through the economy and could become embedded.
"America's inflation problem is bigger than an energy shock," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union.
The large upward increase in GDP came from revisions to investment as well as consumer and government spending.
Consumer spending, which accounts for about two-thirds of all economic activity, rose 4.2% in the third quarter. A metric known as real final sales to private domestic purchasers, which Fed officials regard as a key indicator of underlying demand, jumped 5.8%, reflecting an upward revision of 0.9 percentage point.
In other economic news Wednesday, the Labor Department reported that initial jobless claims slipped to 189,000 for the week ending Nov. 21, down 13,000 from the prior week and back to around the lowest level since the late 1960s. Wall Street had been expecting 200,000.

Goldman Sachs Sees U.S. Natural Gas Demand Surging on Data Center Boom
Data center proliferation will drive demand for natural gas in the United States over the next two years, Goldman Sachs has forecast, estimating that some 52 GW of new data center capacity could be added to the grid in 2028 alone.
"Year-to-date, data-center power capacity and demand have increased by nearly 30% in the US, contributing to more than one third of US total power demand growth," the bank's analysts wrote in a note this week, as cited by Reuters. "We expect growth acceleration in data centers to be driven not only by a higher volume of facilities, but by increasingly larger physical footprints and higher power density," they said.
This will drive stronger growth in demand for electricity and, by extension, for natural gas, which has become the preferred method for data center operators to source reliable, baseload electricity since nuclear takes too long to build.
That data centers are massive energy demand sources is no news. Indeed, data centers are the primary reason for upbeat demand growth projections in the natural gas industry. U.S. gas-fired power generation capacity in development directly tied to data centers nearly doubled to 189 GW in the first half of the year, and chances are the momentum continued in the second half as well. Data center operators like natural gas. And natural gas producers like data centers.
No wonder, then, that U.S. natural gas production is on track to close a second consecutive year with record-high natural gas output as producers respond to demand signs both at home and overseas.
Soaring demand for powering data centers combined with rising liquefied natural gas exports amid expanding liquefaction capacity, as well as surging global demand for spot LNG cargoes in the absence of Qatar's gas due to the Iran war, is pushing American natural gas production higher this year.

items.content:
US Stock Futures Fall as AI Sector Volatility Returns Ahead of Key PCE Inflation Data: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
US equity futures declined on Wednesday as renewed concerns surrounding artificial intelligence investments weighed on technology stocks, while investors awaited the latest US inflation figures for indications of the Federal Reserve's next monetary policy decision.
Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL) raised its annual revenue forecast following strong demand for AI servers, although its shares declined in premarket trading. Meanwhile, reports of potential new US tariffs and falling oil prices remained in focus.
Nasdaq Futures Lead Declines as Technology Shares Remain Under Pressure
At 08:05 GMT, Nasdaq 100 futures were down 491 points, or 1.9%, while S&P 500 futures declined 72 points, or 1%. Dow Jones futures fell 251 points, equivalent to 0.5%.
US Treasury prices advanced, pushing the benchmark 10-year yield down to approximately 4.86%, potentially reflecting increased demand for defensive assets. The US dollar strengthened, while gold prices declined.
"It's pretty wild out there at the moment," analysts at Deutsche Bank said in a research note.
Artificial intelligence-related stocks experienced significant volatility over recent sessions. Concerns about the sustainability and potential returns of AI investments triggered a sell-off late last week, followed by a sharp recovery on Monday after Jensen Huang returned as chief executive of Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA).
However, the recovery proved short-lived, with both the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 declining on Tuesday as concerns surrounding the sector resurfaced.
Nvidia surrendered part of its recent gains and continued to trade lower ahead of Wednesday's opening bell.
Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT), the developer of the Claude chatbot, also erased the initial 34% gain recorded following its stock market debut last week, with its shares weakening further in premarket trading.
"[I]nvestors decided to fade the Jensen-induced tech squeeze from Monday as most people realize the sector's problems didn't stem from that single incident but instead reflect a whole range of questions and concerns, many of which are still very much in place," analysts at Vital Knowledge said in a note.
Market attention is shifting towards the latest US economic indicators, particularly October's Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, one of the Federal Reserve's preferred measures of inflation.
Economists expect the index to increase by 0.3% month on month, following a previous rise of 0.5%.
Estimates from alternative inflation data provider Truflation point to an annual increase of 3.8%, considerably above the Federal Reserve's 2% inflation target.
The central bank raised interest rates in October for the first time since 2023, with several policymakers subsequently signalling that further monetary tightening may be necessary to address persistent inflationary pressures.
Higher energy costs associated with the ongoing conflict involving Iran have contributed to inflation remaining elevated.
Although markets widely anticipate another interest rate increase in December, some investors believe recent volatility across AI-related stocks could encourage policymakers to adopt a more cautious approach to further monetary tightening.
Dell Raises Annual Revenue Forecast to $202 Billion
Dell Technologies increased its full-year financial outlook for the third time this year, supported by growing demand for servers used in artificial intelligence data centres.
The company now expects revenue of approximately $202 billion for the financial year ending in January, compared with its previous forecast of $192 billion.
AI server sales are expected to account for approximately $78 billion of total annual revenue. Dell had previously increased its financial guidance in May and September.
"We see Dell as the overall server leader with leading OEM AI server share," analysts at Mizuho said in a research note.
Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke reported that Dell ended the quarter with a record AI-related order backlog of $132.3 billion, having secured $60.2 billion in new orders.
However, elevated development costs associated with artificial intelligence products are expected to put pressure on profitability within the company's server division during the current quarter.
Despite the improved revenue outlook, Dell shares traded lower ahead of the US market opening.
US Administration Reportedly Preparing Additional Tariffs
Investors are also monitoring reports that the United States is preparing to introduce new tariffs on imports from several trading partners, including China and the European Union.
According to Bloomberg News, the Trump administration is considering additional tariffs to replace previous broad-based measures that were struck down by the US Supreme Court.
The Office of the US Trade Representative is reportedly preparing to conclude an investigation into excess manufacturing capacity under provisions of a 1974 trade law that allows the president to impose tariffs in response to unfair trade practices.
According to the report, the proposed measures would not increase overall tariff rates beyond levels already established under individual trade agreements, including those negotiated with China and the European Union.
Deutsche Bank analysts said that, for equity markets, "matters weren't helped by the latest tariff headlines".
Brent Crude Extends Losses Despite Middle East Tensions
Oil prices continued to decline on Wednesday, with Brent crude falling below $91 per barrel and US West Texas Intermediate also weakening.
Signs of increasing crude oil supplies outweighed concerns about renewed attacks on commercial shipping around the Strait of Hormuz.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported further incidents involving commercial vessels, while Iranian media separately reported another incident involving an oil tanker.
Iran has threatened to tighten its control over the strategic waterway until its demands are addressed, including the removal of the US blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets.
US Vice President JD Vance held discussions with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani regarding regional developments, although negotiations between Washington and Tehran remain unresolved.
NBC News also reported that US officials were considering potential action against Iran's senior leadership. Regional tensions extended to Saudi Arabia following a reported Houthi attack in Riyadh that injured 11 people.
Despite continued geopolitical uncertainty, crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf have increased in recent months.
A key price spread for Dubai crude, the Middle East's benchmark, also shifted into a bearish market structure this week, indicating that near-term supplies were exceeding demand.

items.content:
Will China Get Access to Nvidia's AI Chips? Huang's Return Intensifies US-China Technology Battle
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's return to the helm of the world's most valuable chipmaker has intensified a growing political battle in Washington over China's access to advanced artificial intelligence technology.
An Nvidia logo and a computer motherboard appear in this illustration taken August 25, 2025. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's return to the helm of the world's most valuable chipmaker has intensified a growing political battle in Washington over China's access to advanced artificial intelligence technology. Although US President Donald Trump intervened to restore Huang's position, the decision has increased pressure from lawmakers who argue that allowing China to obtain powerful American semiconductors could undermine US national security.
Nvidia reinstated Huang as chief executive on Monday following his resignation over revelations about extramarital relationships, including one involving Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed who has been accused of having links to Chinese intelligence.
The decision was welcomed by investors but triggered criticism among US lawmakers from both parties. Some officials have argued that Huang's return raises broader questions about the relationship between America's technology industry, the Trump administration and national security policy towards China.
Nvidia shares fell more than 7% on Tuesday after rising sharply on Monday following news of his reinstatement.
MD Briefing delivers expert analysis across five global fronts — the Indo-Pacific, energy, geoeconomics, European security, and the Middle East — every Monday morning. Free.
Why Is Nvidia's China Business Becoming a US National Security Issue?
The controversy has revived a fundamental disagreement in Washington over how the United States should compete with China in artificial intelligence.
One position, supported by business figures close to Trump, including Huang, favours allowing Chinese companies to purchase advanced American chips. Supporters argue that maintaining access to Nvidia technology could make China's AI industry dependent on US suppliers and reduce Beijing's incentive to develop competing domestic alternatives.
The opposing position is held by China hawks in Congress and parts of the administration. They argue that restricting access to advanced semiconductors is essential to preventing Beijing from strengthening its artificial intelligence capabilities, particularly because Nvidia and AMD produce some of the world's most advanced AI chips.
Senator Tom Cotton, the Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, has warned that China could obtain advanced American chips through smuggling and remote access.
He argued that the controversy involving Nvidia and Megaspeed represented only part of a much wider national security challenge, adding that Huang's reinstatement did not resolve those concerns.
Huang is scheduled to be interviewed by Congress next week, placing Nvidia's leadership and its position on Chinese chip access under further scrutiny.
Trump Defends Huang as Washington Faces Growing Pressure
Trump celebrated Huang's return on Monday, taking credit for the decision during an interview with CNBC and describing the Nvidia chief executive as a national treasure.
The president said the company's board had examined whether Huang's position created a national security problem and concluded that it did not.
Trump's intervention has nevertheless intensified criticism from lawmakers who want tighter restrictions on China's access to American technology.
The administration had already taken a relatively conciliatory approach to China compared with the previous restrictions introduced under Democratic President Joe Biden. In December, Trump approved the sale of Nvidia's advanced H200 artificial intelligence chips to China, a decision that attracted criticism from both Democrats and Republicans.
Supporters of the policy argue that selling American chips to China could preserve US technological influence and discourage Beijing from relying entirely on domestic manufacturers.
However, critics believe that access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors could accelerate China's AI development and weaken the effectiveness of American export controls.
Despite Huang's return, recent developments suggest that Washington's approach to Chinese technology companies may be moving towards tighter restrictions.
The Commerce Department added Megaspeed and several other companies to a US trade blacklist on Monday, preventing American businesses from supplying them with chips and other technology.
The administration has also tightened licensing requirements for certain semiconductor shipments and overseas data centres serving Chinese companies.
Aaron Friedberg, a professor of politics and international affairs at Princeton University, expects the controversy to generate further pressure on the administration to strengthen existing restrictions.
He argued that Trump's intervention could trigger a broader political reaction extending beyond Nvidia and China's access to semiconductors.
Another concern influencing Washington's calculations is the possibility of Chinese retaliation. Beijing could respond to tighter technology restrictions by expanding controls on rare earth mineral exports, which are essential for electronics, artificial intelligence hardware and military equipment.
However, some analysts argue that China is already seeking to reduce its dependence on American technology.
Michael Schiffer, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, said Beijing wanted Chinese companies to use domestic alternatives such as Huawei chips rather than Nvidia products. He argued that China's reluctance to purchase American chips had recently become a significant obstacle to US export ambitions, alongside existing restrictions.
Three US Bills Could Further Restrict China's AI Chip Access
The debate is also moving through Congress, where three proposed bills could significantly strengthen restrictions on China's access to advanced semiconductors.
The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress greater authority over advanced chip exports. The Chip Security Act would require companies to track their semiconductors to prevent smuggling, while the MATCH Act would encourage US allies to restrict China's access to advanced chipmaking equipment.
The MATCH Act could prove particularly sensitive for Beijing because it would involve Washington seeking to influence the technology policies of allied countries. China views restrictions on its technological development as a major challenge to its economic and strategic ambitions.
Paul Triolo, technology policy lead at advisory firm DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, warned that the proposed measures could undermine the existing US-China trade truce.
He argued that Beijing could retaliate strongly against new restrictions, potentially creating another cycle of escalation that would damage bilateral relations.
The legislation could also reshape the political balance in Washington. Even if the proposals do not pass before the end of 2026, Democrats are expected to control large majorities in both chambers of Congress after January 3. Together with Republican lawmakers who favour a tougher approach towards China, they could potentially secure enough votes to override a presidential veto.
How Will China Respond to Washington's Chip Restrictions?
Beijing is unlikely to base its long-term technology strategy on the possibility of continued access to American semiconductors.
Lizzi C. Lee, an expert on technology and the Chinese economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said China was unlikely to rely entirely on Trump's goodwill or the policies of a future US president.
She expects the latest controversy to strengthen China's efforts to replace foreign technology with domestic alternatives, particularly in the artificial intelligence sector.
This strategy could accelerate investment in Chinese semiconductor manufacturers and AI hardware developers, reducing the country's exposure to American export restrictions over time.
For Washington, this creates a difficult policy dilemma. Restricting access to advanced chips could slow China's technological progress in the short term, but it could also encourage Beijing to invest more aggressively in developing independent alternatives.
Huang's return may have resolved Nvidia's immediate leadership uncertainty, but it has not settled the wider dispute over China's access to advanced American technology.
His upcoming congressional interview, the progress of proposed export-control legislation and the administration's decisions on semiconductor licensing will help determine the direction of US policy.
The broader challenge for Washington is balancing commercial interests with national security concerns while avoiding measures that could trigger damaging retaliation from Beijing.
For China, the controversy reinforces the importance of developing domestic semiconductor capabilities rather than relying on American suppliers. Even if US restrictions remain limited, uncertainty surrounding future administrations could accelerate Beijing's efforts to build an independent AI technology ecosystem.
The Nvidia controversy therefore extends far beyond one company's leadership. It reflects a deeper struggle over who will control the technologies shaping the global economy and whether the United States can maintain its semiconductor advantage without accelerating China's drive for technological independence.

360 News Desk , Crude inventories , crude oil storage , EIA
U.S. commercial crude oil inventories ( excluding those in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve ) increased by 1.1 million barrels from the previous week.  At 418.9 million barrels, U.S. crude oil inventories are 3% below the five-year average for this time of year, according to the EIA crude oil and petroleum weekly storage data, reporting inventories as of November 20, 2026.
Summary of weekly petroleum data for the week ending November 20, 2026
U.S. crude oil refinery inputs averaged 17.3 million barrels per day during the week ending November 20, 2026, which was 428,000 barrels per day more than the previous week’s average. Refineries operated at 97.5%  of their operable capacity last week.
Gasoline production last week averaged 9.7 million barrels per day.
Distillate fuel production decreased, averaging 5.2 million barrels per day.
U.S. crude oil imports averaged 6.2 million barrels per day last week, increased by 673,000 barrels per day from the previous week. Over the past four weeks, crude oil imports averaged about 6.2 million barrels per day, 5.8% more than the same four-week period last year.
Total motor gasoline imports (including both finished gasoline and gasoline blending components) last week averaged 314,000 barrels per day, and distillate fuel imports averaged 103,000 barrels per day.
Total motor gasoline inventories increased by 1.7 from last week and and are about 3% above the five year average for this time of year.
Distillate fuel inventories increased by 0.7 from last week and are about 6% below the five year average for this time of year.
Propane/propylene inventories decreased 1.0 million barrels from last week and are 11% above the five year average for this time of year.
