US Semiconductor Stocks Extend Losses as AI Investment Concerns, Tariff Risks and Rate Expectations Weigh on Markets
Semiconductor ©Adobe Stock Images US semiconductor and technology hardware stocks came under renewed selling pressure in premarket trading on Wednesday as investors reassessed the potential returns from artificial intelligence infrastructure investments amid rising borrowing costs and renewed trade uncertainty.
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) declined 5.3% to $147.20, while Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) fell 5.9% to $592.88 and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) dropped 5.7% to $389.69.
Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL) lost 7.4%, Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) declined 3.8% and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) fell 3.9%.
Nasdaq 100 futures were down approximately 2%, while S&P 500 futures declined 1% and Dow Jones futures slipped 0.4%.
Semiconductor Sector Extends Tuesday's Sharp Declines
Wednesday's premarket losses followed a substantial sell-off across semiconductor stocks during Tuesday's regular trading session.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 7.9%, while Nvidia shares declined 5.9%. Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices also recorded significant losses.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.5%, although the Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 0.9%, reflecting the concentration of selling pressure within technology and artificial intelligence-related stocks.
The recovery recorded on Monday following Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive proved short-lived, as investors returned their attention to the financial sustainability of AI infrastructure spending.
Financing Risks Raise Questions Over AI Investment Returns
Investors are increasingly assessing whether substantial debt-financed investments in data centres and computing infrastructure will generate sufficient financial returns to support current technology sector valuations.
The Wall Street Journal reported growing concerns surrounding financing risks, with widening credit spreads and increasing costs of insuring technology company debt against default contributing to investor caution.
Expectations of higher interest rates have added to these concerns, particularly for highly valued growth companies and businesses undertaking substantial capital expenditure programmes.
Potential US Tariffs and Inflation Data Add to Market Uncertainty
Trade policy uncertainty has emerged as another source of pressure on technology shares.
The Office of the US Trade Representative is preparing to publish findings from an investigation into alleged excess industrial capacity across 16 major trading partners, including China and the European Union.
The investigation could provide a basis for additional US tariffs.
Meanwhile, investors are awaiting Wednesday's US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation report, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure, alongside third-quarter gross domestic product figures.
Money markets were pricing in a 96% probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate increase at the Federal Reserve's December meeting.
NAND Flash Price Forecast Highlights Memory Market Risks
Additional uncertainty emerged within the semiconductor memory market following a forecast from industry research firm TrendForce.
The firm indicated that NAND flash contract prices could begin declining in early 2027 as weaker orders from Chinese cloud service providers and expanding production capacity potentially push the market into oversupply.
Despite continued demand for advanced computing infrastructure, semiconductor stocks remain under pressure from concerns surrounding AI investment returns, financing conditions, trade policy and the outlook for memory component pricing.

items.title: Fox News Hosts Clash Live on TV Over Donald Trump’s Iran War - Newsweek
items.summary: Fox News Hosts Clash Live on TV Over Donald Trump’s Iran War  Newsweek
items.content:

Fox & Friends co-hosts Brian Kilmeade and Rachel Campos-Duffy clashed during Wednesday’s broadcast over President Donald Trump ’s war with Iran , with Campos-Duffy arguing that voters had rejected the conflict and Kilmeade defending the decision to confront Tehran.
The exchange comes weeks after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, as the war's cost and direction remain politically contentious. Their dispute highlighted a broader split on the right over Trump’s foreign policy and whether the conflict has undermined the domestic agenda that helped return him to the White House.
The disagreement sharpened when Kilmeade argued that confronting Iran had long been a U.S. priority. “Your list. Not mine!” Campos-Duffy interjected after Kilmeade said the Iran issue had been “on the top of everyone’s list for 35 years.”
Brian Kilmeade and Rachel Campos-Duffy Clash Over Iran War
The dispute began during a discussion of Trump’s planned meeting with Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and the potential for cooperation between the president and the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress. Kilmeade envisioned a scenario in which Democrats tried to use government or military funding as leverage to force Trump to dismiss Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or withdraw from Iran.
Lawrence Jones called such demands a “non-starter,” and Kilmeade agreed. Campos-Duffy immediately challenged him, asking whether he meant the war itself was a non-starter. Kilmeade replied: “That’s just the beginning of it,” arguing that demands framed as ultimatums would put Trump “in a corner” rather than create room for negotiation.
Campos-Duffy offered a different political reading. She argued that opposition to the war was one area where populist factions on the left and right found common ground in the midterms. Trump, she said, could potentially capitalize on those overlapping constituencies to work with Democrats during the next two years.
“The president is a populist,” Campos-Duffy said. “And there is populism on the left. And there is populism on the right. And there are some places where this overlaps.”
Trump’s Midterm Strategist Outlines What Republicans Need to Change
The disagreement reflects a deeper foreign-policy divide within Trump’s political coalition, according to Jon Hoffman, a research fellow at the Cato Institute and adjunct professor at George Mason University.
“Foreign policy represents one of the deepest fissures on the political right and the Iran war brought this to the forefront,” Hoffman told Newsweek .
Hoffman distinguished between MAGA, which he described as “a brand and a cult of personality around a single individual,” and the broader America First movement that helped propel Trump to the presidency.
“The Iran war was the antithesis of America First and has fractured the Trump coalition,” Hoffman said. “It was a war of choice launched on behalf of Israel despite no imminent threat to the security, prosperity, or freedom of the American people.”
His comments mirror a central tension in the Fox exchange. Campos-Duffy argued that opposition to the war extended across the political spectrum and later told Kilmeade that the conflict had “cost us the Trump agenda.” Kilmeade rejected that assessment, arguing that Iran had presented a problem that U.S. leaders had needed to address for decades.
Hoffman said the political repercussions extend beyond the disagreement over the war itself, arguing that the conflict has drawn the administration away from other priorities.
“The America First constituency is tired of endless wars in the Middle East ,” he said. “Even from a perspective of Trump’s own interests, this war was foolish: It has pulled attention and resources away from his other priorities and now represents his legacy.”
He also pointed to Republicans ’ midterm losses as a warning about the political consequences of prolonged military involvement.
“The midterms should be a wake-up call for Republicans: Endless wars are not just bad policy; they are bad politics,” Hoffman said. “They should push for a swift end to this disastrous conflict.”
The disagreement grew more pointed when Kilmeade defended the rationale for confronting Iran, invoking decades of concern over Tehran and the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, the nuclear agreement reached between Iran and world powers during the Obama administration.
“Addressing the Iran situation has been on the top of everyone’s list for 35 years,” Kilmeade said, before beginning to discuss the JCPOA.
Kilmeade acknowledged the distinction but continued, describing the nuclear agreement as a “disaster” and arguing that someone eventually had to address the Iran issue. Campos-Duffy countered with the political cost she believes Trump has paid for doing so.
“Well, it cost us the Trump agenda, sadly,” she said.
“Well, it is the debate of the century right now,” he said before moving the program to another segment with Carley Shimkus.
Iran War Has Become a Political Liability for Trump
The argument unfolded against the backdrop of a conflict that began when the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28, following months of tensions and negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear program.
Fighting has continued through periods of ceasefire and diplomatic negotiations, while attacks around the Strait of Hormuz and across the Persian Gulf have disrupted global energy and commercial shipping.
The war has also imposed high financial costs. The Defense Department told Congress in November that U.S. military spending on the conflict had reached at least $48.3 billion.
The conflict became a major issue in this month’s midterm elections, when Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. The BBC cited polling showing 63 percent of Americans surveyed said the United States was wrong to start the war, while an NBC News exit poll found 74 percent of voters considered the conflict a crucial or major factor in their vote. The results underscored the political pressure surrounding the conflict and help explain why Campos-Duffy characterized opposition to the war as an issue that could cross ideological lines.
Trump has repeatedly defended his handling of Iran and maintained that military pressure was necessary to address the country’s nuclear and security threat. The administration has simultaneously pursued diplomatic contacts with Tehran, though a June agreement failed to produce a lasting end to hostilities.
Fox Hosts Previously Sparred Over Russia and Ukraine
Wednesday was not the first time Kilmeade and Campos-Duffy publicly split over Trump’s approach to a major international conflict. The pair had another heated discussion on Fox & Friends in October, this time over Russia, Ukraine and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
During the October 11 exchange, Campos-Duffy pointed to Trump’s suggestion that Ukraine might need an election and potentially a new leader. She accused Zelensky of taking actions that hurt Trump politically despite what she described as the administration’s generosity toward Ukraine’s war effort.
Kilmeade challenged that line of argument and raised the implications of penalizing countries for purchasing Russian energy. The exchange reflected the same underlying foreign-policy divide that resurfaced Wednesday: whether Trump should prioritize confronting U.S. adversaries abroad or limit American commitments that parts of his political coalition see as expensive distractions from a domestic populist program.
The Iran disagreement, however, carries an additional political dimension because Campos-Duffy explicitly linked the conflict to Trump’s ability to enact his agenda after the Republican midterm losses. Kilmeade rejected that connection outright.

A new poll has found that a majority of voters in the United States want an end to the US-Israel war on Iran immediately, even if it means accepting less favourable conditions.
Overall, 55 percent of those surveyed agreed with an “end to the war now, regardless of the terms”.

That number was even higher among Democrats and independents, who agreed with the statement at a rate of 80 percent and 59 percent, respectively. About 25 percent of Republicans said the same.
A majority of Democratic voters also supported steps to pressure the administration of President Donald Trump to stop the conflict.
Fifty-three percent of party members said they would favour Congress withholding funding for military operations, and 51 percent would back an “an Iran war-funding cutoff” in upcoming budget negotiations, even if the manoeuvre risked a government shutdown.
The numbers were published on Tuesday as part of the latest Critical Issues Poll, released by the University of Maryland and the research firm Ipsos.
Shibley Telhami, the poll’s principal investigator, said he was surprised by the level of support for ending the war, regardless of the terms.
“We knew that people were strongly opposed to this war and wanted it to end,” he told Al Jazeera in a phone call. “What we were less sure of is what they would be willing to accept to achieve this.”
The survey asked 1,022 US adults about their perspectives on the war.
In one question, they were tasked with assessing with three options: whether to end the conflict immediately, escalate militarily, or continue on the current path in order to extract concessions from Iran.
Just 21 percent of all respondents favoured the current path, and 18 percent supported escalation.
“Clearly, the public mood is to end it now, whatever it takes,” said Telhami.
Voters also appear sceptical about the US government’s arguments in favour of the war, which include dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme.
The Critical Issues Poll found that only 28 percent of those surveyed believed that the war had left Iran in “worse position” to develop nuclear weapons.
While the US has long voiced concerned that Iran could pursue nuclear arms, intelligence assessments have not found evidence that Tehran has authorised such a step since abandoning its nuclear weapons programme in 2003.
The Strait of Hormuz has also emerged as a key issue, with Iran closing the waterway to commercial traffic early in the war. The Trump administration has responded with a naval blockade in the strait.
Some 20 percent of the world’s oil supply passes through the maritime artery, and fuel prices have spiked as a result of the war.
About 35 percent of respondents in Tuesday’s poll said that they believe Iran is now in control of the strait, while just 12.7 percent said the US is in control.
The poll comes as the Democratic Party is debating how far it should go to end the unpopular war.
In the recent midterm elections , backlash against the war — and as well as related issues like rising fuel prices — contributed to big gains for the Democratic Party.
Trump’s Republican Party, meanwhile, suffered one of its most bruising setbacks in modern US history, losing control of both chambers of Congress.
Members of the Democratic Party’s anti-war left have pointed to the results as proof that voters want an end to the war and an end to US support for Israel.
But that position has brought them into conflict with members of the party’s more hawkish establishment wing.
While leaders such as Representative Hakeem Jeffries and Senator Chuck Schumer have both expressed support for ending the war, they have yet to commit to aggressive strategies to reach that goal.
That includes potentially cutting off funding for military operations against Iran, or using an upcoming funding battle in December to demand that the White House end the war.
“A lot of Democratic figures are dismissing the intensity of public feeling on this issue,” said Telhami. “If they don’t adapt, they will be left behind.”
He added that progressive figures such as Senator Bernie Sanders and Senator Chris Van Hollen have been among those pressing for a more assertive stance.
Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer to lead the Democratic majority in the US Senate, has used the war to portray the party’s moderate leadership as out of step with voters.
The poll found that Democratic voters prefer Van Hollen over Schumer by a ratio of nearly three to one.

items.title: Liesman: Nvidia whiplash tests Kevin Warsh’s push to read market signals
items.summary: The extreme market gyrations and the drama surrounding Nvidia this past week have highlighted the dilemma facing Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh.
items.content:
Nvidia whiplash tests Kevin Warsh’s push to read market signals — Liesman
The extreme market gyrations of the past week highlight the dilemma facing Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh.
Warsh has said he wants to use market indicators more than forecasts to guide policy, but those indicators can be subject to extreme volatility.
Which market signals are worth watching, and for how long do they need to persist to guide policy?
Fed's Warsh faces inflation vs. market-driven rate dilemma: Here's what to know
The extreme market gyrations and the drama surrounding Nvidia this past week have highlighted the dilemma facing Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh .
On Friday, as stocks sold off, market-based probabilities that the Fed would raise interest rates declined. On Monday, with Jensen Huang back in office , a powerful rally restored market confidence that two more rate hikes are coming.
On one level, ignoring daily market vicissitudes and focusing on the long term is at the heart of one of the key changes Warsh wants to push through at the Fed. On another, he has been explicit that markets do a better job of forecasting and he wants to use market indicators more than forecasts to guide policy.
But those indicators can be subject to extreme volatility.
Take the benchmark Goldman Sachs Financial Conditions Index. Last week, the market decline and widening of credit spreads had sent a signal for the Fed to ease back on at least some of its plans to tighten policy. Some Fed commentators called for rate hikes to be taken off the table entirely. On Monday, the index eased by 22 basis points, reversing nearly half of the prior week's tightening, and both December and January hikes were back on the table.
Warsh's message, in words and deeds, is for markets to look beyond that volatility. He traveled to San Francisco last week and patiently presided for three hours over a conference on the outlook for artificial intelligence and its potential economic impact , peppering economists and tech leaders with questions about the dangers and potential upside of AI for the economy. The meeting was part of the AI task force he has convened that, in turn, is one of five to study different areas of Fed policymaking.
Peterson: Here’s what Bessent’s about-face on Jensen Huang reveals about Trump and China
Consumer confidence shoots up after Democrats’ midterm victories — though inflation worries persist
Warsh wants Fed officials to talk less. Instead, they're talking more
In his opening remarks , he said, "These groups are a way of broadening our thinking, of inviting robust discussions that take us far deeper... than fleeting data points [or] daily market moves. Our task forces are an intellectual investment to help better equip us for the next policy conjuncture and beyond."
Compare that desire for intellectual investment to Warsh's press conferences after Fed meetings. He has cut them down to a half hour, and he routinely spends much of the time parrying reporter questions about what the next Fed move will be, part of his general aversion to forward guidance. At the June press conference, he paraphrased former Secretary of State George Schultz saying, "Press conferences are useful. But when you have one, you want to make sure you have something important to say." In a regime where Warsh does not want to provide forward guidance, there is far less to say than there once was.
Here's what is known of what Warsh seems to believe about monetary policy:
Most forecasts, especially those from economic models and Wall Street economists, are bad. They are not just bad, but injurious to policymaking because they lead to the wrong policy and can lock the forecaster into the expected outcome.
Much of the data that goes into those models are of poor quality, including antiquated inflation indexes, spending data that is simulated from surveys and rickety measures of output.
The best forecasts come from market expectations derived from measures of inflation compensation, credit spreads, stock indexes and Treasury interest rates — to name just a few he is known to follow.
The Fed and Wall Street spend too much time thinking about the next meeting or the meeting after that and too little time deliberating the broad economic forces that will shape the economy and guide interest rates a year or two down the road.
Inflation is not the result of tariffs, oil prices or the massive AI build-out. It is the result of policy set by the central bank relative to those developments.
Today's inflation is most likely the result of policies enacted as much as nine months to a year ago, and is itself reflected in data that is also out of date.
The cure for this is for the Fed to talk less, decide less and deliberate more.
In a sense, it seems, Warsh wants to make monetary policy the way he did his old job at the Duquesne Family office working for legendary investor Stan Druckenmiller. There, he evaluated startup companies, many of them with the wisp of an idea in the mind of a tech geek, for the possibility of profit many years down the road. Marked to market, those investments would show big negative numbers on the day's profit and loss statement. Down the road, some would go bankrupt and others would offer handsome returns.
Warsh's focus on AI highlights his dilemma in wanting to do policy in a different, more forward-looking and market-based way. The outlook for AI, as the chairman himself has admitted, is moving rapidly and is deeply uncertain. Markets may already be rethinking the potential earnings upside and the amount that will be spent on the AI buildout. The adoption rate of the technology is uncertain, and so are the economic effects on inflation and growth.
Warsh in San Francisco showed a particular interest in the potential for a "China Shock" to hit jobs in the U.S. service sector, a reference to how Chinese imports devastated the U.S. manufacturing sector earlier this century. If that happened, widespread unemployment could lead the Fed to lower rates over time, while the frenzied AI buildout looks now to be sparking inflation and pressuring rates upward. So there are different messages for the Fed chairman being sent from the same economic development.
It is established in the monetary policy literature that the current rate level affects the economy with what are known as "long and variable lags." Those lags mean that where policy is set today will influence the economy sometime next year. The objective is to set policy for where one thinks the economy will be next year.
Wide error bands surround most economic forecasts, including those from the Fed. But there are similarly wide error bands on market pricing. The question is, which market signals are worth watching, and for how long do they need to persist to guide policy? The Nvidia situation shows markets can be very short-term about the long-term signals they send.

items.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return shows the U.S.-China AI race is about more than chips
items.summary: Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO demonstrates that the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not just about semiconductors, but tech talent too.
items.content:
Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return highlights U.S.-China AI talent race
Donald Trump said China might have tried to recruit Jensen Huang after his Nvidia exit, in a CNBC interview about the Nvidia CEO's reinstatement.
Recruiters and analysts interviewed by CNBC said Chinese technology companies are aggressively competing for experienced AI engineers in the U.S. and Asia.
Sources said access to advanced AI chips, research resources and compensation can influence where engineers choose to work.
Students Experience Virtual Reality At National Science Popularization Event In Nanning
China News Service | China News Service | Getty Images
BEIJING — Jensen Huang ' s return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent.
"We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China.
The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research.
Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack."
Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging.
Huang reinstatement reignites voter angst over tech's outsized power
Jensen Huang's Nvidia return highlights U.S.-China AI talent race
Nvidia whiplash tests Kevin Warsh's push to read market signals: Liesman
AI debt worries grow as Nvidia rebound masks Big Tech spending squeeze
Jensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession plan
Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington
AG Blanche, FBI's Patel dodge questions about Huang investigation
Jensen Huang to face Congress the same day as Nvidia GTC
Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., during a Bloomberg Television interview in London, UK, on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026.
More than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models.
Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday.
"He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said.
"Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China.
Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention.
For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China.
As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added.
Already, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations.
In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive.
Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country.
It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore.
Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S. ," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups.
She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options.
"There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI."
However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one.
She also noted Huang's "deep belief in America" and laws that would block him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese company.
The U.S. has restricted China's access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors over the last four years. But in early 2025, DeepSeek upended assumptions that chip restrictions could keep Chinese AI capabilities well behind that of the U.S.
A few years ago, only the U.S. and Singapore had the kind of AI talent that Chinese companies were looking for, Wu said. "Today we see the gap has been filled," she said, adding the supply of local talent has increased in the last two to three years.
"The demand is huge," Wu said, saying one ex- Alibaba AI engineering candidate with seven years of experience had more than five offers.
Switching between companies can result in a 25% to 30% pay bump, Wu said. She expects the trend to persist for another two years, although the increase in compensation may not be as high.
Still, restricted access to advanced AI chips plays a role in where the best researchers choose to work.
It's a question of "where I can do my further research and do I have enough resources to do my research," said Lu.
He said industry research suggests "China is becoming a really important pool for talent, while the U.S. is paying 80% of the money."
